                                                                                    Languages and ethnic groups

                                                                                    Main articles: Languages of China and List of ethnic groups in China

                                                                                    The PRC legally recognizes 56 distinct ethnic groups. The largest of these are the Han Chinese, who constitute more than 91% of the total population. The minority groups are generally found in the western and border regions of China.[296] Social and wealth inequalities exist between many minority groups and the Han, especially in the rural southwestern areas.[297]

                                                                                    Most Han are speakers of Mandarin Chinese, of which Standard Chinese is a standardized form and the official language of the PRC.[298] Around 300 million people speak other Chinese languages (often described as dialects in Chinese sources). While also written with Chinese characters, these are not highly mutually intelligible with Mandarin or each other. The primary branches of Chinese are Mandarin, Wu, Yue (Cantonese), Min, Gan, Hakka, and Xiang; the latter six are mainly spoken in Southern China. Since the 1950s, local dialects have steadily assimilated into Mandarin or one of the main regional registers.[298]

                                                                                    Simplified Chinese characters, first standardized in the 1950s, are used to write Chinese throughout mainland China, while traditional Chinese characters remain in use in the SARs and Taiwan.[299]Hanyu Pinyin is the official romanization system for Chinese in the PRC.[300]

                                                                                    Other language families are found throughout China.[301] Distantly related to Chinese, Tibeto-Burman languages are found in the west and southwest.[302] In southwestern China, many Hmong–Mien and Kra–Dai languages are spoken by minority groups. Offshoots of the Austroasiatic and Austronesian language families are also found in the south in smaller numbers. In the northwest, Turkic (including Uyghur) and Mongolic languages are found, as well as two Indo-European languages (Russian and Tajik).[301] Several endangered Tungusic languages are found in northwestern and northeastern China.[303] Since the 2010s, the Chinese government has intensified linguistic assimilation policies, generally requiring schools to use Standard Chinese as the primary language of instruction.[304]

                                                                                    Religion

                                                                                    Main article: Religion in China
                                                                                    See also: Irreligion in China and Antireligious campaigns in China

                                                                                    The Chinese religious tradition is heavily syncretic, incorporating various folk religious practices alongside Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism. These 'three teachings' were the three main institutionalized schools of Chinese religion. These exist alongside introduced minority religions such as Christianity and Islam,[305][306] as well as various new religious movements.[307] Statistics on affiliation are difficult to gather due to complex and varying definitions of religion and the diffusive nature of local traditions.[308] Many people follow religious teachings and practices without considering themselves adherents.[308]Local deities are commonly worshiped along widely-known gods, including figures such as Guan Yu and Mazu.[309]

                                                                                    Confucianism is a philosophical and spiritual tradition that originated in the Eastern Zhou, emphasizing the study of the classics and the relations of the individual, society, and heaven.[310][311] Following Western influences, it has sometimes been identified as a religion.[310] Daoism emphasizes the Dao ('way') as the world's origin and fundamental force, and seeks to harness it through spiritual cultivation. Initially a philosophical movement during the Eastern Zhou, the religious tradition of Daoism emerged during the 2nd century CE.[312][313]Mahayana Buddhism was introduced to China during the Han dynasty and spread rapidly over the following centuries. Although it was often dismissed by the Confucian literati, Buddhism greatly influenced other Chinese religious and philosophical traditions.[314]

                                                                                    Although the PRC and CCP are legally atheist, freedom of religion is formally guaranteed by the Chinese constitution.[308] The PRC officially recognizes five religions: Buddhism, Taoism, Islam, Catholicism, and Protestantism. Formal religious practice is managed by "patriotic associations" for each of the recognized faiths overseen by the CCP's United Front Work Department.[315] However, the majority of religious activities take place outside of these registered organizations.[316][317] The PRC has attempted to crack down on some forms of unregistered religious practice, such as Protestant house churches. Religious practices among minority groups, such as Islam among the Uyghur and Tibetan Buddhism, have come under close state scrutiny and regulation over fears of separatism.[317]

                                                                                    Education

                                                                                    Main articles: Education in China and Higher education in China
                                                                                    See also: Literacy in China

                                                                                    Following an optional two to three years of preschool, China has nine years of free compulsory education, generally with six years of elementary school and three years of junior high school.[318] If they pass entrance examinations, students may then attend a senior high school, choosing between an academic or vocational track.[319] The gaokao exams allow access to undergraduate higher education, with additional examinations required to attend postgraduate programs and achieve a master's or doctoral degree.[319] As of 2022, 95% of junior high students continue to high school, while higher education has a 59.6% enrollment rate.[320]

                                                                                    As of 2022, China had 158 million students enrolled in compulsory school, and 46.5 million enrolled in higher education. There are over 200,000 elementary and junior high schools, over 22,000 secondary schools, and over 3,000 colleges and universities.[321] Both private and public schools exist at all levels, with 10.6% of elementary and junior high students attending private schools.[322]Its academic publication apparatus became the world's largest publisher of scientific papers in 2016.[323]

                                                                                    Health

                                                                                    Main article: Health in China
                                                                                    See also: Medicine in China and Pharmaceutical industry in China

                                                                                    The vast majority of primary health care institutions in China offer both allopathic and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). In 2017, there were approximately 9,000 community health centers in urban areas—which oversaw roughly 25,000 health stations—and 37,000 township health centers in rural areas. There were about 639,000 village clinics, which operate as independent, for-profit enterprises subsidized by the state.[324][325]

                                                                                    The National Health Commission, together with its counterparts in the local commissions, oversees the health needs of the population.[326] After the beginning of the reform and opening up in 1978, the health of the Chinese public improved rapidly because of better nutrition, although many of the free public health services provided in the countryside disappeared. Healthcare in China became mostly privatized, and experienced a significant rise in quality.[327] China is a major producer and exporter of active pharmaceutical ingredients.[328]

                                                                                    According to 2025 state data, the life expectancy at birth exceeds 79 years,[329] and the infant mortality rate is 4 per 1,000.[330] Rates of stunted growth declined from 33.1% in 1990 to 4.5% in 2024.[331] Mental health services are underfunded and unevenly distributed, with most services in provincial capitals and the more developed eastern provinces.[332] Following the 2003 SARS outbreak, the World Health Organization found the biosafety standards at Beijing's National Institute of Virology to be inadequate.[333] The COVID-19 pandemic was first identified in Wuhan.[334]

                                                                                    Culture

                                                                                    Main articles: Chinese culture and Culture of the People's Republic of China

                                                                                    Beginning in the Qin and Han dynasties and continuing over the following millennia, an area of Chinese cultural influence grew to encompass much of East Asia. Japan, Korea, and Vietnam adopted various political, philosophical, religious, and aesthetic concepts from China, boosted by their adoption of Chinese characters and participation within the tributary system.[335]China has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the Great Wall and Grand Canal. This is the second-most of any country (behind Italy).[336] Chinese culture has historically emphasized family connections, with filial piety and the veneration of ancestors seen as vital duties under Confucian ethics. Prior to the 20th century, family relations were highly patriarchal, and arranged marriages were commonplace.[337]

                                                                                    Prior to the adoption of the Gregorian calendar in 1912, China traditionally used a lunisolar calendar of 12 months.[338] The 60-part sexagenary cycle was often used to enumerate days as well as years,[339] alongside the twelve-year Chinese zodiac.[340]Major holidays and festivals in China include the Chinese New Year (or Spring Festival), the Qingming Festival, the Mid-Autumn Festival, and National Day.[341]

                                                                                    Art

                                                                                    Main article: Chinese art

                                                                                    Elite culture of the imperial period saw skill in art as a marker of refinement and high social status.[342] Renowned art pieces often bear inscriptions and seals from their previous owners, allowing for the tracing of provenance over long periods of time.[343] Traditional Chinese art makes use of a wide array of common motifs, metaphors, and symbols, often using nature as allegory.[344]

                                                                                    Chinese paintings are traditionally made with ink brushes on paper or silk.[342] Horizontal handscrolls and vertical hanging scrolls are common formats, alongside wall paintings, folding screens and hand fans.[345]Calligraphy, emerging during the 3rd and 4th centuries CE, was traditionally regarded in China as the most prestigious form of art, and remains among the most widely practiced.[346][347] Western genres and techniques of painting gained popularity in China during the early 20th century,[348] while the People's Republic promoted art as a means to embody socialist ideals during the Mao era.[349] The 21st century has seen a boom in the production and international influence of Chinese contemporary art.[350]

                                                                                    Pottery and metal crafts in China date to ancient times.[351]Porcelain, also known as china, became a common form of ceramic during the 7th century.[352] By the 14th century, it became popular to decorate porcelain vessels with elaborate blue and white patterns, which became the most popular and widely recognized form of Chinese ceramics.[353]Jade crafts and lacquerware have been popular decorative mediums since ancient times.[354]

                                                                                    Architecture

                                                                                    Further information: Chinese architecture

                                                                                    Wood is the most commonly used material in traditional Chinese architecture. Roofs of important buildings, generally ceramic tile, are often ornate and hipped.[355] Traditional buildings are often arranged around cardinal directions, with grandeur expressed through large complexes, often featuring courtyards and large gates.[356] The spiritual concept of feng shui influences the layout of houses and settlements, seeking to orient them around the flow of qi, vital energy.[357]

                                                                                    Pagodas, multi-story religious towers far taller than other forms of traditional architecture, were introduced to China alongside Buddhism, and comprise many of China's oldest buildings.[358] Western-style architecture was introduced by Europeans during the 19th century,[359] while domestic architects began to implement Western design principles in the 20th.[360] The reform era has seen a boom in the construction of contemporary skyscrapers and office buildings, largely supplanting traditional architecture.[361]

                                                                                    Performing arts

                                                                                    Further information: Music of China

                                                                                    The music of China is highly diverse and regional.[362] Traditional Chinese music uses a wide variety of instruments, including the dizi (a flute), erhu (a bowed string instrument), guqin (a plucked string instrument), guzheng (a plucked zither), pipa (a lute), sheng (a mouth organ), suona (a wind instrument), and various types of bells and drums.[363][364] Western-style music and conservatories spread during the early 20th centuries, leading to the Chinese orchestra to develop as a fusion of Western orchestral music with Chinese instruments. Western classical music remains highly prestigious.[365] Inspired by Western jazz and boosted by the introduction of recording studios, Mandarin pop music emerged in Shanghai in the 1920s, while the folk rock-inspired Cantopop became popular around Hong Kong during the 1970s.[366] After reform and opening up, various forms of pop and rock music reached widespread popularity across mainland China.[367]

                                                                                    Chinese opera emerged from shuochang, folk traditions of narrative singing. By the Yuan dynasty, separate forms of opera existed in the north and south.[368] Influenced by various regional traditions and kunqu, a genre popular during the Ming dynasty, Peking opera reached national popularity during the Qing dynasty,[369] while various local and regional forms of opera emerged across the country.[368] During the Mao era, the PRC promoted revolutionary opera and communist-oriented folk music.[370]

                                                                                    Chinese dance has evolved for millennia, and by the Han period was a frequent subject of art and poetry, as well as an element of religious rites.[371] Dancers often performed for the imperial courts,[372] while the popularity of dance in Chinese opera led to increasing numbers of dance troupes across all levels of society during the Qing.[373] Western dances gained popularity in the early 20th century, while the CCP promoted folk dances such as yangge.[374]

                                                                                    Cuisine

                                                                                    Main article: Chinese cuisine

                                                                                    Chinese meals generally incorporate a grain (fan) alongside meat or vegetable-based dishes (cai). Flour—as steamed buns, dumplings, pancakes, or noodles—is the primary grain in the north, alongside maize, millet, rice, and in some regions, sorghum. Rice—steamed or in the form of congee, rice noodles or rice cakes—dominates in the south. Although Chinese cuisine is highly diverse and regional, pork, chicken, fish, and duck tend to be the most common meats.[375][376][377] Soybeans are a common staple across China, made into products such as tofu and soy sauce.[378]Stir frying in woks is the most common cooking method, alongside deep-frying, steaming,[379] and hot pot, where dishes are cooked in simmering broth at the table.[380]

                                                                                    People in China generally eat three meals a day,[381][382] often with a simple breakfast and a more elaborate dinner.[383]Chopsticks are the main eating utensil.[384] Dishes are usually served to be shared among multiple people, rather than served in individual portions.[382] Hot tea almost always accompanies meals across the country, in lieu of water. Alcoholic drinks such as rice wines and the distilled liquor baijiu are commonly served with meals.[385] Chinese cuisine was traditionally divided into four great traditions: Lu (Shandong), Yang (Jiangsu), Chuan (Sichuan), and Yue (Guangdong). Fujian cuisine is sometimes listed in lieu of Yang.[386][387] Chinese Buddhists have developed a unique cuisine that avoids meat, while Chinese Islamic cuisine excludes pork and alcohol.[388][389]

                                                                                    Fashion

                                                                                    Main article: Chinese clothing

                                                                                    Various forms of robe served as the main form of clothing for both men and women throughout Chinese history, changing and adapting over the centuries. New dynasties often sought to reform formal clothing.[390] Silk, hemp, and later cotton were the main textiles.[391] Both men and women generally bound their hair with caps or pins, except during periods where foreign hairstyles were enforced by the ruling elite.[390]

                                                                                    Chinese fashions changed greatly during the 20th century, as traditional designs largely gave way to western clothing.[392]Qipao became a popular form of women's dress during the early 20th century, but are today rare outside of formal occasions.[393] After a focus on simple, practical clothing during the Mao era,[394][395] the reform era saw the emergence of a Western-style fashion industry.[396] In the 21st century, the Hanfu movement has sought to promote a reconstructed form of traditional Chinese clothing.[397]

                                                                                    Literature

                                                                                    Main articles: Chinese literature and Chinese poetry

                                                                                    China has among the longest continuous literary traditions in the world.[398] The Late Shang-era oracle bone inscriptions are the oldest known Chinese writing,[30] while the oldest surviving literary works—such as the Book of Documents—date to the early Zhou.[399] The Chinese literary canon was historically centered of the Five Classics (a diverse set of ancient transmitted texts) and the Four Books (central Confucian texts).[400] The traditional literati regarded literature as didactic in purpose, with fiction seen as useless and potentially corruptive.[401][402] However, poetry was viewed highly for its ability to convey the nature of reality. The poetry of the Tang era was particularly prized by later dynasties.[403][404]

                                                                                    Classical Chinese was the standard literary register until the early 20th century, when it was overtaken by written vernacular Chinese.[405] Before this, fiction was generally written in vernacular Chinese, and literary works were generally written in Classical Chinese.[406] Popular vernacular literature spread with the introduction of printing, resulting in works such as the Four Classic Novels of the Ming and Qing periods.[407]

                                                                                    Modern Chinese literature has been heavily influenced by the political upheavals of the 19th and 20th centuries, seeking to explain the contemporary political climate or imagine its future.[408]New Culture writers promoted the importance of fiction and vernacular Chinese experimented with new modernist forms,[409] while writers of the Reform era sought to explain the trauma of the Mao era and Cultural Revolution.[410]

                                                                                    Media

                                                                                    Main article: Mass media in China

                                                                                    China's largest media company is China Central Television, which competes with various provincial television networks. China is the largest online video market, with its major streaming platforms including iQIYI, Youku, and Sohu.[411] As of 2025, Chinese film industry is the second largest by global box office earnings (behind the United States), although 98% of these earnings are from domestic consumers. The PRC limits the number of foreign films which can be shown domestically. According to state sources, China has over 90,000 movie screens as of 2025, the most of any country.[412]

                                                                                    As of 2023, China has over 2,600 radio stations, all state-owned, and over 1,900 newspapers. Cities generally have a newspaper published by the local government, and another by the local CCP branch. Journalism is tightly controlled and monitored by the CCP, with content critical of the government prohibited. Foreign Chinese-language news outlets are blocked, while English-language outlets are occasionally available but often censored. Prominent newspapers in China include the CCP's People's Daily and the state-run Global Times, China Daily, and Reference News.[411] The most popular social media platform in China is WeChat. Other major platforms include the microblogging service Weibo, the news and content aggregator Toutiao, the video-sharing platform Xigua Video, and Douyin, the Chinese version of the short-form video platform TikTok.[413]

                                                                                    Sport and games

                                                                                    Main article: Sport in China
                                                                                    Further information: Video games in China

                                                                                    Traditional sports such as martial arts and dragon boat racing have been practiced in China for over a millennium.[414] The ball game cuju predates the Qin dynasty and remained popular for millennia, declining during the late Qing dynasty. Chuiwan (similar to modern golf) and polo were popular sports among elites throughout portions of the imperial period, while commoners played various regional ball games.[415][416] Modern sporting was introduced to China from the West during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. China first attended the Olympic Games in 1932.[417]

                                                                                    The PRC began to invest heavily in elite sports during the 1990s, and in 2008 Beijing hosted the Summer Olympics.[418] Elite sports in China are managed by the General Administration of Sport, which oversees management centers for various sports, as well as provincial sports committees and teams. The vast majority of sports funding, especially for elite sports, comes from the government.[419] China hosted the Winter Olympics in 2022,[420] and the Asian Games in 1990, 2010, and 2022.[q][422] China is dominant among international competition in table tennis (often dubbed China's national sport),[423][424]badminton, diving, and weightlifting,[424][425] and is among the top global competitors in snooker.[426]

                                                                                    Various card, dice, and board games gained popularity in imperial China, most notably weiqi (also known as Go) and xiangqi (a relative of chess).[427]Mahjong emerged during the 1800s, initially one of many popular gambling games.[428] China is the world's largest video game market. Video games were introduced from Japan in the 1980s, and online video games grew to immense popularity alongside the spread of the internet.[429]
